one_line: A compliance-by-default design, signage, notice and retention service for NJ small businesses deploying cameras/audio/sensors — sold as risk reduction and documentation, never as a surveillance outcome promise.

problem.summary: Small NJ operators are buying cheap cloud cameras and AI analytics faster than they are buying rules for them. The typical 5-200 staff business has cameras with no written policy, no signage, no retention limit, no audio decision (microphones left on), no employee notice, no biometric policy, and no procedure for what a manager may do when an alert fires. In New Jersey that combination is legally exposed on four fronts at once: (1) the Wiretapping Act makes unconsented capture of a conversation the recorder is not party to a third-degree crime plus civil damages; (2) the hidden-camera statute criminalises recording in places with a reasonable expectation of privacy and imposes a specific signage rule for retail fitting rooms; (3) the Law Against Discrimination, per DCR's January 2025 guidance, reaches algorithmic discrimination including tools built by a third-party vendor; and (4) the FTC's Rite Aid case shows the federal failure mode — the FTC alleged that an unmanaged AI flagging system generated thousands of false-positive matches, fell hardest on customers in plurality-Black and Asian communities, and the settlement ended in a five-year facial-recognition ban plus notice, deletion and complaint-response duties (complaint filed Dec 19, 2023; stipulated order entered Feb 26, 2024; the separate 2010 data-security order modified by the Commission Mar 5, 2024). A separate NJ duty already bites anyone with a service van or truck fleet: written notice before using a vehicle tracking device, $1,000 first / $2,500 subsequent penalty. Today this is handled by hand — a manager's memory, a vendor's generic PDF, or nothing at all.

evidence.fact: N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d) permits a private person to intercept an oral communication only if they are a party or one of the parties gave prior consent, and never for a criminal, tortious or other injurious purpose; the subscriber to a phone is not consent for conversations they are not on.

Illegal recording of an in-person conversation is a third-degree crime (3-5 years, up to $15,000), and civil plaintiffs may recover the greater of actual damages, $100/day or $1,000, plus punitive damages, attorney's fees and costs (N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-24).

N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9 makes it a third-degree crime to record another person's intimate parts, or fourth-degree for undergarment-clad intimate parts, where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed; observing a fitting-room access way/foyer is only lawful with conspicuous posted notice at the entrance (subsection e), and subsection f makes it a violation of subsection a. or b. to observe or record a person in a private dressing stall. Subsection d separately supplies an affirmative defense to a crime under the section where the actor gave prior notice and acted with a lawful purpose, so the defensible design reading — no cameras in stalls — is a design conclusion, not a statutory carve-out.

P.L. 2021, c.449 (N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22), approved Jan 18, 2022, penalises an employer who knowingly uses a tracking device in a vehicle used by an employee without written notice: up to $1,000 first violation, up to $2,500 each subsequent, collectible by the Commissioner of Labor and Workforce Development.

FTC v. Rite Aid: the FTC's complaint filed Dec 19, 2023 alleged a 2012-2020 AI facial-recognition deployment produced thousands of false-positive matches, that employees acted on those alerts by following, searching, ejecting and publicly accusing wrongly flagged customers, and that the system was more likely to false-positive in plurality-Black and Asian communities. A stipulated order was entered Feb 26, 2024 in E.D. Pa.; it bars facial recognition/analysis in its stores for five years and requires consumer notice, written complaint response, and deletion of biometric data within five years. The Commission separately modified the 2010 data-security order on Mar 5, 2024 to give the settlement effect.
evidence.year: 2023 complaint; Feb 26, 2024 stipulated order entered; Mar 5, 2024 modification of the separate 2010 order

evidence.fact: The FTC's May 2023 Policy Statement on Biometric Information treats undisclosed, unavoidable biometric collection as potentially unfair under Section 5, and unsubstantiated claims about accuracy, fairness or real-world performance (including claimed theft reductions) as deceptive.

New Jersey DCR's January 2025 guidance states that the LAD applies to algorithmic discrimination in employment, housing, places of public accommodation, credit and contracting, and that a covered entity may be held liable for discrimination resulting from an automated decision-making tool it did not develop. The guidance states it imposes no new or additional requirements and is not enforced as a substitute for the LAD.

The New Jersey Data Privacy Act defines 'biometric data' to exclude ordinary photographs and audio/video recordings unless the data is generated to identify a specific individual — so plain CCTV is outside that definition while facial recognition is inside it; the Act also only applies to controllers processing 100,000+ consumers (or 25,000+ with data sale revenue).

Retail trade recorded 306 fatal work injuries in 2023, 123 of them from violent acts (94 homicides, about 30% of the sector's fatalities); accommodation and food services recorded 84 violent-act fatalities.

Middlesex County in 2024 had 2,282 retail trade establishments (37,019 employees), 1,752 accommodation and food service establishments (24,124 employees), 5,036 health care and social assistance establishments (57,733 employees) and 1,305 transportation and warehousing establishments (49,911 employees), out of 25,042 establishments and 376,330 covered jobs in the county.

buyers.business_type: Independent retail (convenience, grocery, hardware, apparel, smoke/vape, pharmacy-front)
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 1-5 locations, 5-100 staff; matters from the first location with a register and a stockroom
buyers.why: Highest camera density, highest false-accusation exposure, most likely to have bought cloud cameras without a policy; shrink and violence data drive the purchase.

Cameras over POS and back door, tip-dispute and wage-hour claims, alcohol-service incidents, and staff break areas where audio mics create wiretap exposure; 84 violent-act fatalities in accommodation and food services in 2023.

buyers.business_type: Pharmacies and clinics (independent pharmacy, dental, urgent care, physical therapy)
buyers.why: Rite Aid is the sector's cautionary tale. NJ covered health care facilities must also run a written violence-prevention program with an annual comprehensive risk assessment (N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5.20), and N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.7(a)2 requires at least annual walk-through surveys of all worksite areas that identify physical-environment risk factors — at a minimum physical layout, access restrictions, surrounding crime rate, 'non-working alarm systems, communication devices, surveillance cameras and/or mirrors', and poor lighting/visibility. The statute itself does not mention cameras; the regulation's camera reference is as a risk factor to be surveyed, not a control to be specified. Note that 'covered health care facility' is a statutory category, so a small independent practice may or may not fall inside it (inference, unconfirmed).

Cameras are mandatory, not optional: N.J.A.C. 17:30-9.10 requires Commission-approved video covering all critical control activities, remote viewing access, a 30-day archive, and 24/7 monitoring of alarm and video systems.

buyers.business_type: Auto dealers, repair shops and any business with service vans/trucks
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 5-200 staff with at least one employee-used vehicle
buyers.why: Dash cams and GPS trackers trigger the NJ written-notice duty with a per-violation penalty; most small fleets have no written notice at all.

Fastest-growing sector in the county (+26.1% employment 2018-2024); dock/yard cameras plus driver-facing cameras plus FMCSA overlay, and the largest concentration of sensor and video data with no retention policy.

existing_solutions.product: R120 / R200 dome cameras with cloud console
existing_solutions.what_it_does: Cloud-managed IP cameras with AI features sold as a separate licence tier; 10-year camera warranty.
existing_solutions.pricing: R120: $399 hardware + $149 per-camera Professional licence = $548 first year (MSRP); the pricing page does not state the licence term (it says cameras 'require an ongoing license' and are sold through resellers with 'flexible payment options'), and AI features and cloud archiving are excluded from that licence

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Low-cost PoE camera feeding a local UniFi Protect NVR; the default 'cheap and local' option for small shops.
Cloud-first cameras, doors, intercoms and alarm sensors on one console; hardware MSRP published, per-camera licence required in addition.
existing_solutions.pricing: Hardware MSRP published on the pricing page (e.g. TD33 intercom $1,699, AL54 locks $1,399-$1,799, alarm sensors $99-$199); camera-level licence price not published on that page — Unknown, by quote

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Local, on-premises NVR with real-time object detection, zones, tracked-object events, semantic search on thumbnails (0.15) and built-in face recognition (0.16, optional and off by default).
existing_solutions.pricing: Free / open source; hardware cost only

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Edge TPU dongle used as a Frigate detector for local inference on a small NVR/mini-PC.
existing_solutions.pricing: $111.00 at reseller Seeed Studio (SKU 114991790); Google's coral.ai is now a developer landing page that lists no consumer price, and availability varies by reseller

existing_solutions.what_it_does: The default real-time person/object detector family behind most small-site video analytics.
existing_solutions.pricing: AGPL-3.0 free, or commercial Enterprise licence (custom quote); closed-source or commercial deployment requires the Enterprise licence per Ultralytics' published terms

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Nobody sells the thing the buyer actually needs: an audio-off-by-default design, a fitting-room and break-room exclusion map, an NJ signage and employee-notice set, a written retention/deletion schedule, a no-face-recognition default with a documented opt-out, and a written false-positive escalation procedure a manager can follow.

gap_for_local_installer: The camera vendors sell hardware and generic 'AI'; the FTC and DCR sell enforcement. Between them sits an unserved job: designing a camera/audio/sensor deployment that is defensible in New Jersey by default, and documenting it. Concretely — audio capture disabled unless a posted-notice/consent scheme exists; no cameras aimed at fitting rooms, dressing stalls, restrooms or locker areas (and none in or into a private dressing stall at all, given N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9(f) and the ambiguity of the (d) notice defense); a written employee monitoring notice (plus a separate vehicle-tracking notice); a written retention and deletion schedule; facial recognition off unless the client signs a documented assessment and consumer-notice package modelled on the Rite Aid order; and a one-page 'what to do when an alert fires' procedure that forbids confronting or accusing a customer on the strength of a model output. That layer is process plus configuration, it is repeatable across 2,282 retail and 1,752 food-service establishments in Middlesex County, and it is the part a remote SaaS vendor cannot install or sign. One unverified gate sits under this: New Jersey is reported to license alarm/security businesses (N.J.S.A. 45:5A-23 et seq.; N.J.A.C. 13:31A), and it is reported that installing or servicing CCTV/electronic security systems falls inside that scope, but I could not render the Division of Consumer Affairs advisory-committee FAQ to confirm it (it returns an Incapsula challenge). Until that is confirmed with the state, treat licensing as a precondition of taking any install work, not as a footnote: the defensible position is to partner with a licensed firm rather than install directly.

technical_approach.established_pattern: RTSP cameras -> on-premises NVR (Frigate) -> edge detector (YOLO-family on Coral/NPU/GPU) -> multi-object tracking -> zone and line-crossing rules with schedules -> event clip + metadata written to local storage under a fixed retention window -> optional small vision-language model invoked only on exception clips to produce a short factual description for a human reviewer. Audio is off by default. Face recognition is off by default. Everything stays on the LAN so no customer imagery leaves the building, which shrinks the FTC Section 5 and NJDPA surface and makes the retention promise technically true rather than contractual.

models_and_tools.role: Local NVR + object detection + zones + retained event clips; face recognition exists but stays disabled by default for NJ deployments

models_and_tools.name: Ultralytics YOLO11
models_and_tools.role: Person/vehicle/object detector on the edge; AGPL or paid Enterprise licence depending on how the deliverable is shipped

models_and_tools.name: Google Coral USB Accelerator
models_and_tools.role: Low-cost Edge TPU detector for a small on-site box (Frigate 'edgetpu' detector)

models_and_tools.name: Qwen3-VL (2B / 4B variants)
models_and_tools.role: Small vision-language model for describing exception clips in words ('two people, one carrying an unbagged item, exit door, 21:14') instead of shipping a classifier label

models_and_tools.name: LFM2.5-VL-3B (Liquid AI)
models_and_tools.role: Edge-oriented VLM (LFM2.5 backbone + SigLIP2 vision encoder) for on-box visual grounding and short captions where a 3B model fits the hardware budget

models_and_tools.name: Cactus
models_and_tools.role: On-device inference engine for phone-class hardware — relevant for a manager-side review app that never uploads footage

hardware.item: Cloud camera alternative (Rhombus R120, hardware + first licence)
hardware.approx_cost: $548 (MSRP: $399 hardware + $149 licence; licence term not stated on the page)
$111 at reseller Seeed Studio (Google's own product page no longer lists a price)

hardware.item: Commercial on-prem appliance comparator (Rhombus N100 Relay, up to 10 cameras)
NVR host (small-form-factor PC with 8-16 GB RAM; Frigate recommends 8 GB+ for semantic search)
hardware.approx_cost: Roughly $300-$700 retail (inference — component prices vary by supplier; no single source opened for this line)

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: No for the 90% case. Person/vehicle detection, zone rules, line-crossing, dwell time and after-hours alerts all work with off-the-shelf detectors plus site calibration (zones, schedules, confidence thresholds, minimum object size). Fine-tuning only becomes worth it for site-specific classes the base models do not have — e.g. a spill, a pallet left in a fire aisle, a specific cart type — and even then the cheaper first move is prompting a small VLM on exception clips rather than training a detector. Anything that would identify a person should be treated as out of scope by default given the Rite Aid order and NIST's demographic false-positive findings.
technical_approach.data_needed: Two to four weeks of recorded clips per camera to calibrate zones and thresholds; 200-500 labelled frames per custom class if fine-tuning is attempted; a written inventory of camera locations and fields of view (for the privacy map); the client's existing employee handbook and any vehicle-tracking notice; and a signed retention schedule so deletion can be evidenced.

measured_outcomes.finding: CCTV produced a modest but statistically significant crime reduction of about 13% versus control areas, with the strongest effects in car parks and residential settings and stronger results where cameras were actively monitored or bundled with other interventions; the authors caution against CCTV as a stand-alone measure.
measured_outcomes.sample: 76 studies, 40-year systematic review with meta-analysis (Piza, Welsh, Farrington & Thomas, Criminology & Public Policy 18(1))

measured_outcomes.finding: Many face-recognition algorithms showed false-positive rates 10-100x higher for Asian and African American faces than for Caucasian faces in one-to-one matching, with elevated false positives for African American women in one-to-many identification; results varied widely by algorithm.
measured_outcomes.sample: Nearly 200 algorithms from nearly 100 developers (NISTIR 8280, FRVT Part 3: Demographic Effects)

measured_outcomes.finding: The FTC alleged that an unmanaged AI facial-recognition flagging system generated thousands of false-positive matches over an eight-year deployment; that employees, acting on those alerts, followed, searched, ejected and publicly accused wrongly flagged customers; and that the system was more likely to false-positive in stores located in plurality-Black and Asian communities. These are allegations in a complaint resolved by a stipulated order, not adjudicated findings. Outcome: a five-year ban on facial recognition/analysis plus consumer notice, written complaint response, deletion of images/models, and biometric deletion within five years.
measured_outcomes.year: 2023 complaint; stipulated order entered Feb 26, 2024; 2010 order modified Mar 5, 2024
measured_outcomes.sample: One retailer (FTC alleges hundreds of stores), 2012-2020 deployment, Eastern District of Pennsylvania

measured_outcomes.finding: Retail trade recorded 306 fatal work injuries in 2023, of which 123 were violent acts and 94 were homicides (about 30% of the sector's fatalities); accommodation and food services recorded 84 violent-act fatalities.
measured_outcomes.sample: National census of fatal occupational injuries (CFOI), all US workplaces

measured_outcomes.finding: Shrink was reported at 1.6% of sales, or $112.1 billion industry-wide for FY2022 (up from 1.4% and $93.9 billion in 2021); NRF subsequently stopped publishing an industry-wide shrink rate because retailers calculate it differently, so this figure is the last comparable benchmark and should not be treated as current.
measured_outcomes.sample: 177 retail brands accounting for $1.6 trillion of 2022 retail sales and 97,000+ US locations; senior loss-prevention executives surveyed online — not a probability sample of small business

measured_outcomes.finding: A deep-learning anomaly-detection framework reported 83.59% accuracy on the UCF-Crime shoplifting subset with its best classifier (LogReg), alongside precision 82.46%, recall 84.62% and F1 83.53% (Table 3 of the preprint) — a 0.11-point gain over the best single CNN (MobileNetV2, 83.48%), i.e. roughly one in six cases still misclassified within that benchmark evaluation, which says nothing about live-store false-alarm rates. The 87.25% 'unseen dataset' figure is a separate violence-detection test on a movie dataset: the authors state they could not obtain shoplifting footage for that test. All figures here are read from the arXiv preprint v1 (17 Jul 2024); the journal version returned HTTP 403 and was not readable.
measured_outcomes.year: 2024 (arXiv preprint v1, July 2024); journal version 2025, not readable
measured_outcomes.sample: Two public benchmark datasets (50 shoplifting + 50 normal clips sampled from UCF-Crime; RLVS violence) plus a movie clip set for the unseen test; one model configuration

measured_outcomes.finding: DCR's guidance cites a Rutgers survey finding that 63% of surveyed New Jersey employers use one or more AI-enabled tools to recruit or make hiring decisions, while 47% agreed such tools might lead to unfair outcomes.
measured_outcomes.year: 2024 survey (Liu et al.), cited in Jan 2025 guidance
measured_outcomes.sample: Survey of New Jersey employers; sample size not stated in the guidance

legal_privacy.issue: Audio recording of conversations (the microphone in the ceiling camera)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d): a private person may intercept an oral communication only if they are a party, or one of the parties gave prior consent, and not for a criminal/tortious/other injurious purpose. A shop owner is not a party to customer-to-customer or employee-to-employee conversations, so unconsented audio capture in a retail or break area is exposure, not a feature.

legal_privacy.issue: Criminal and civil penalties for unlawful recording
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Third-degree crime punishable by 3-5 years and up to $15,000; civil recovery of the greater of actual damages, $100/day or $1,000, plus punitive damages, attorney's fees and costs under N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-24.

legal_privacy.issue: Cameras in restrooms, changing areas and fitting rooms
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9: third-degree to record intimate parts, or a person engaged in a sexual act, where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed; fourth-degree for undergarment-clad intimate parts. Subsection (f) makes it a violation of subsection a. or b. to observe or record a person in a private dressing stall of a retail fitting room. Subsection (d) supplies an affirmative defense to a crime under the section where the actor posted or otherwise provided prior notice of intent and acted with a lawful purpose, so whether any notice could cure a stall recording is not answered by the statute's text — a lawyer should confirm; the defensible design is no cameras in or aimed into stalls.

N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9(e): observing or recording a person in the access way, foyer or entrance of a fitting/dressing room is lawful only if the actor conspicuously posts prior notice at the entrance; disclosure of such images is restricted to law enforcement, subpoena/court order, or co-workers/managers within the scope of employment. Subsection (f) does not extend this signage allowance into the stall itself.

legal_privacy.issue: Employee vehicle tracking (dash cams, GPS, telematics)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22 (P.L. 2021, c.449): written notice required before an employer knowingly uses a tracking device in a vehicle used by an employee; up to $1,000 first violation, up to $2,500 each subsequent. Applies to employee-used vehicles, not just employer-owned ones, and does not supersede FMCSA rules.

legal_privacy.issue: Employee monitoring notice for video-only workplace cameras
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: No New Jersey statute requiring written notice for ordinary video-only workplace cameras was confirmed. Notice can still be required by a union agreement, employment contract or the employer's own policy, and privacy expectations still constrain placement (2C:14-9). Treat 'we don't need notice' as unverified.

legal_privacy.issue: Biometric data and facial recognition under NJ's comprehensive privacy law
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: P.L. 2023, c.266 defines 'biometric data' to cover facial mapping/geometry/templates used to identify a specific individual, and expressly excludes ordinary photographs and audio/video recordings unless the data is generated to identify someone. 'Sensitive data' includes biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person. The Act only applies to controllers processing 100,000+ consumers (or 25,000+ with data-sale revenue) and 'consumer' excludes persons acting in an employment context.

legal_privacy.issue: Algorithmic discrimination and vendor-built tools under the NJ Law Against Discrimination
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: DCR's January 2025 guidance: the LAD applies to automated decision-making tools in employment, housing, places of public accommodation, credit and contracting; poor design, training or deployment can produce discrimination; a covered entity may be liable for discrimination from a third-party tool it did not develop. DCR states the guidance creates no new or additional requirements and is not enforced as a substitute for the LAD, and describes its examples as illustrations of legal theories rather than per se violations. The guidance's training-stage example is the FTC's Rite Aid allegations (low-quality enrollment images, disproportionate false positives); its deployment-stage example is the now-discontinued PredPol predictive-policing algorithm and the feedback loop it produced.

legal_privacy.issue: Facial recognition in retail: federal enforcement template
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: FTC v. Rite Aid — complaint filed Dec 19, 2023; stipulated order for permanent injunction entered Feb 26, 2024 by Judge Hodge in E.D. Pa.; the Commission modified the separate 2010 data-security order on Mar 5, 2024 to give it effect. Terms: five-year ban on facial recognition/analysis in stores, pharmacies and online retail platforms; notice to consumers enrolled in a biometric database and to consumers acted against based on system output; written investigation/response to complaints; deletion of images and models derived from them; biometric information deleted within five years; independent assessments and CEO certification. The theory is Section 5 unfairness (failure to assess/mitigate foreseeable harm, low-quality enrollment images, no accuracy testing, no employee training) plus a 2010 order violation. All findings are allegations the FTC made in the complaint, settled by consent — not adjudicated.

FTC Policy Statement on Biometric Information (May 18, 2023): unsubstantiated claims about a biometric technology's validity, reliability, accuracy, fairness or efficacy are deceptive — including claims that are true only for some populations, or based on tests that do not replicate real-world conditions; undisclosed or unavoidable biometric collection can be unfair. Note: the claim carried over from the earlier draft that the FTC's October 2025 regulatory agenda proposed rescinding this statement was not confirmed against any FTC page in this revision and should be treated as unverified.

No general NJ retention limit for small-business CCTV was confirmed. Two concrete anchors: cannabis licensees must keep a 30-day video archive and have the system continuously monitored 24/7 (N.J.A.C. 17:30-9.10), and the Rite Aid order required biometric data deletion within five years. Elsewhere, retention is a design choice that becomes a liability if there is no written schedule.

legal_privacy.issue: Signage — fitting rooms and general premises
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey has no general statute mandating 'cameras in use' signs on business premises (not confirmed either way). The one clear statutory camera-signage duty found is the fitting-room entrance notice in 2C:14-9(e).

legal_privacy.issue: Signage — retail food establishment health placard
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.A.C. 8:24-8.12: the operator of every retail food establishment must post the evaluation placard of the most recent health-authority evaluation immediately, in a conspicuous place near the public entrance, so the public may view it.

legal_privacy.issue: Retention — retail food inspection report on premises
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.A.C. 8:24-8.13: the most recent inspection report must be kept on the premises by the operator for public review on request, for a minimum of two years.

legal_privacy.issue: Proposed NJ biometric-surveillance notice requirement (not law)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Assembly Bill 1494 (reported out of the Assembly Consumer Affairs Committee June 3, 2024, 2024-25 session) and its 2026-27 successor A3929 (reported March 19, 2026) would bar a business from using a biometric surveillance system on a consumer at its premises unless it gives clear and conspicuous notice (a sign at the perimeter of the monitored area suffices) and uses it for a lawful purpose; they would also require an explanation of criteria where the system is used to deny entry or remove someone, bar profiting from the data, and make violations consumer-fraud violations penalised at up to $10,000 first / $20,000 subsequent offence with a 30-day cure for a first violation. Neither bill is law. Senate companion bill numbers appeared in search results but the Senate bill pages could not be rendered, so they are not asserted here.

legal_privacy.issue: Labor-law overlay on workplace monitoring (NLRA Section 7)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: NLRB General Counsel Memo GC 23-02 (Oct 31, 2022) argued for a presumptive violation where surveillance/algorithmic management would tend to chill Section 7 activity and proposed requiring disclosure of monitoring tools and their use. Reported as rescinded by GC 25-05 on Feb 14, 2025. The memo was the GC's enforcement position, not Board law; the underlying Section 7 protection against surveillance that coerces employees is statutory and remains the risk to design around.

legal_privacy.issue: Who may install the system (contractor licensing)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's Fire Alarm, Burglar Alarm and Locksmith Advisory Committee framework (N.J.S.A. 45:5A-23 et seq.; N.J.A.C. 13:31A) is reported to require a licence, and a firm business licence with a named qualified individual, for installing/servicing 'electronic security systems' including CCTV. The Division of Consumer Affairs advisory committee FAQ page could not be rendered in this or the earlier pass (it returns an Incapsula challenge), so the CCTV scope is unverified. This is a precondition to quoting install work, not a settled fact.

public: Reviews that name the failure mode without naming the law: 'accused me of stealing', 'followed me around the store', 'manager was watching us on camera', 'creepy cameras in the break room'.
A help-wanted post for 'loss prevention associate', 'asset protection' or 'AP associate' at a business with 1-5 locations — indicates alert volume someone is already trying to manage by hand.
Multiple locations under one owner (2-5 units) — the point where a verbal policy stops working and a written one becomes necessary.
A NJ Cannabis Regulatory Commission licence: video is mandatory, Commission-approved, remotely viewable and 30-day archived, so compliance paperwork already exists to bolt onto.
Any business with a service fleet (vans, box trucks, plumbers, landscapers, delivery) — vehicle-tracking written-notice duty applies today.
Job ads or LinkedIn posts mentioning Verkada, Rhombus, UniFi Protect, Solink or 'AI cameras' — means hardware is in and the policy almost certainly is not.
Store photos on Google/Yelp/Instagram showing dome cameras, a live monitor at the register, or a camera above a fitting-room entrance.

Health-care practices that may be 'covered facilities' under the Violence Prevention in Health Care Facilities Act (written plan, annual risk assessment, annual walk-through survey that must identify non-working surveillance cameras among other physical-environment risk factors) — the compliance artefact may already be half-built.

Municipal health-inspection placard condition (posted placard under N.J.A.C. 8:24-8.12 and on-premises inspection report under 8:24-8.13) as a proxy for operational sloppiness, and an opening line with the owner.
Public LAD/DCR complaints, news coverage of a shoplifting confrontation, or an OSHA 300A log with assault injuries (posted annually in retail/health care).
walk_in: Count the cameras and note which have mic pinholes — audio capability present with no signage is the cleanest opening line.
Look for entrance signage about cameras or audio. Absence is the norm and is the wedge.

Check the aim: any camera pointed at a fitting room, dressing area, restroom corridor, locker area or staff break table is a stop-work finding under 2C:14-9 (and a wiretap question if audio is on); anything aimed into a private dressing stall should come out before the engagement starts.
Is there a live monitor at the register or office? Live watching by staff is where false accusations start.
Ask two questions verbatim: 'how long do you keep the video?' and 'what does a manager do when they think someone is stealing?' No crisp answer on either = qualified.
Ask whether a written monitoring or vehicle-tracking notice was given to staff. Most will say the handbook 'covers it' without knowing.
Note where the recorder lives — a closet, a cloud app on the manager's phone, or nothing at all.
Look at the fitting rooms and back stockroom door for any posted notice; look at the break area for a camera.
Note the fleet in the lot and whether drivers were told in writing about GPS or dash cams.

pilot.scope: One site, one owner, 2-6 weeks, with a week-0 gate: confirm in writing the NJ alarm/electronic-security licensing position for the scope (partner with a licensed firm, or run the engagement as design/configuration and let the licensed firm do the physical install) before quoting. Week 1: privacy and legal-baseline audit (camera map with fields of view, audio capability inventory, fitting-room/restroom/break-area check, existing handbook and vehicle notices, retention as practised versus as written). Week 2: remediation — disable audio at the camera or NVR unless a posted-notice/consent scheme is signed off; reposition or remove any camera with a privacy-sensitive field of view, including anything aimed into a dressing stall; install entrance signage and fitting-room notices; issue written employee monitoring notice and, if applicable, a vehicle-tracking notice. Week 3-4: stand up a local NVR (Frigate) with zone rules for after-hours entry, exit-door, cash-office and stockroom; optional small VLM captioning on exception clips only; write the one-page alert-response SOP that forbids confronting or accusing a customer on the strength of a model output. Week 5-6: retention/deletion schedule in force (14-30 days general; 30 days where a cannabis licence requires it), evidence of deletion, and a handover compliance packet plus a 60-day check-in.
pilot.hardware: 4-8 PoE IP cameras (Ubiquiti G5 Flex at $129 list is the reference build; Rhombus R120 at $399 hardware + $149 licence if the client wants managed cloud), one on-site NVR host with 8-16 GB RAM, optionally one Coral USB Accelerator (about $111 at current resellers) for detection offload, PoE switch and cabling, entrance and fitting-room signage, and a printed/digital compliance packet. No cloud dependency required; face recognition explicitly not installed.
pilot.success_metric: Primary: a signed compliance packet — camera map, audio decision, exclusion-zone confirmation, employee and vehicle notices issued, retention schedule with deletion evidence, and the alert-response SOP acknowledged by every manager. Secondary, measured pre/post: median time to retrieve a requested clip (target under 10 minutes, from whatever the baseline is), number of customer confrontations attributed to camera alerts (target zero), and a 30-point checklist audit score at week 6 versus week 1. Deliberately not a metric: theft reduction, because the credible evidence base for CCTV alone is a ~13% crime reduction in specific settings (Piza et al. 2019) and any small-shop claim would be unfalsifiable.
pilot.cost_range: Roughly $6,000-$15,000 for the six-week single-site pilot (inference, built from sourced component prices plus assumed NJ labour): hardware $1,000-$4,500 (4-8 cameras at $129-$548 each, NVR host ~$300-$700, optional ~$111 accelerator, switch/cabling/signage), professional services $4,000-$9,000 for 5-10 days of audit, install, policy drafting and handover, and $500-$1,500 travel/insurance/admin. Excludes any attorney review of the notice and policy language, and excludes any licensed electrician or alarm-firm subcontract cost if the licensing gate requires one.
pilot.assumptions: Single site under 10,000 sq ft; existing PoE cabling or willing to run new cable; one owner/decision-maker; no union contract; no biometric or face-recognition requirement (if the client insists on FRT the scope, price and legal exposure all change and the answer should probably be no); no cannabis licence (if yes, add 30-day archive and Commission remote-viewing requirements); contractor licensing settled before work starts (unverified — see data_gaps); insurance in place; client signs that the deliverable is compliance documentation, not legal advice.

fit_score.rationale: Demand (13/20): every camera buyer has the exposure, but few small owners wake up wanting a compliance audit — this is a pull-through sale attached to a camera install or an incident, not a stand-alone purchase, and the lack of an enacted NJ biometric-surveillance statute plus the FTC's shifting posture make the federal tailwind softer than it looks. Local buyers (13/15): 2,282 retail, 1,752 food-service, 5,036 health-care and 1,305 transportation/warehousing establishments in Middlesex County alone, plus every licensed cannabis site with a mandatory 30-day archive. Ability to pay (8/15): the target is 5-200 staff independents; a $6-15k pilot is real money against a $548 cloud camera, and the value shows up as avoided loss rather than new revenue, which is the hardest sale there is. Technical feasibility (17/20): this is configuration and documentation on mature open-source components (Frigate, YOLO, Coral) plus a small VLM for exceptions — no novel research, and local-only processing is the safe default. Legal risk (6/15): the deliverable is explicitly not legal advice, which keeps UPL risk bounded, but the consultancy is designing around two criminal statutes and a civil-rights guidance regime and will be named in any dispute; the two 2C:14-9 placement questions are now narrower and better sourced than in the earlier draft (subsection (f) plus the (d) notice defense), but they are still questions a lawyer must answer, and the unverified alarm/security licensing scope could bar install work outright. Resolving licensing with the state is what would justify moving this sub-score up. Defensibility (9/15): the compliance packet and signage set are copyable by any competitor, and the underlying software is free — the durable parts are the licence, the insurance, the local presence and the incident-response reputation, not the technology.

risks: Unauthorized practice of law: writing notice and policy language that interprets NJ statutes for a client. Mitigation: template + attorney review held by the client, and a written scope that says the deliverable is a technical compliance configuration, not legal advice.

Contractor licensing: New Jersey is reported to license alarm/security businesses and to cover CCTV install/service, but the Division of Consumer Affairs advisory-committee FAQ could not be rendered in either research pass, so the scope is unverified. Treat it as a gate: confirm with the Fire Alarm, Burglar Alarm and Locksmith Advisory Committee before quoting install work, or partner with a licensed firm.
Client pressure toward facial recognition or 'known shoplifter' watchlists — the single highest-severity request, and the exact fact pattern in the Rite Aid complaint. Needs a written refusal policy.
False-accusation liability: a model alert that leads a manager to confront a customer becomes the installer's problem in discovery if the SOP and training were thin.

Privacy-sensitive placement errors (a camera that clips a fitting-room entrance or a break table) are criminal-statute territory, not just a customer-service issue — and 2C:14-9(f) reaches observation or recording in a private dressing stall, with the scope of the (d) prior-notice defense untested in the sources opened here.

Regulatory churn: NJ's biometric-surveillance notice bills keep being reintroduced without becoming law — A1494 was reported out of Assembly Consumer Affairs on June 3, 2024 (2024-25 session) (https://pub.njleg.state.nj.us/Bills/2024/A1500/1494_S1.HTM) and A3929 was reported March 19, 2026 (2026-27 session) with $10,000/$20,000 consumer-fraud penalties (https://pub.njleg.state.nj.us/Bills/2026/A4000/3929_S1.HTM). If either passes, perimeter signage for any biometric system becomes mandatory and the compliance baseline moves mid-engagement.
Retention promise versus reality: if the NVR silently keeps footage beyond the written schedule, the client's own documentation becomes the evidence against them.

Ethical/reputational: selling surveillance to small businesses in a county where 36.4% of residents are foreign-born and 48.2% speak a language other than English at home (2024 ACS 1-year estimates, published in the NJDOL Middlesex County report, https://nj.gov/labor/labormarketinformation/assets/PDFs/pub/County%20Reports/Middlesex%20County.pdf) carries a real risk of disparate impact on customers and staff; the design should be biased toward fewer cameras and fewer alerts, not more.
Labour relations: camera expansion in a 50-200 staff workplace can trigger NLRA Section 7 concerns and organising activity regardless of the current GC memo status.
caveats: This is research, not legal advice; every legal point here should be confirmed by a New Jersey employment/privacy attorney before it appears in a client deliverable. Statutory and regulatory text was read from the NJ Legislature's own site or Cornell LII where possible; several contextual items (alarm licensing scope, NLRB memo status, the absence of a general NJ camera-notice statute, the reported 2025 FTC rescission proposal) rest on secondary sources or search summaries and are flagged confirmed:false. Two items that were flagged in the earlier draft are now read at source: N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.7 (the camera reference is to non-working surveillance cameras as a physical-environment risk factor in walk-through surveys) and the precision/recall figures in arXiv 2408.00792 (82.46%/84.62%, Table 3). The Rite Aid findings are FTC allegations in a complaint settled by stipulated order, not adjudicated findings, and are rated Low. Prices are vendor list/MSRP as published and exclude tax, shipping, installation and any dealer discount; Rhombus does not state its licence term publicly; Coral's own site no longer publishes a price, so a reseller price is used. Cloud licences recur and should be modelled as recurring cost. Vendor claims about AI accuracy or theft reduction were not tested and are rated Low. Nothing here identifies any individual business, owner or employee.
data_gaps: NJ Division of Consumer Affairs alarm/security licensing FAQ would not render (Incapsula challenge on multiple attempts); the claim that CCTV installation requires a licence is unconfirmed and is the single most important open question for the business model.

The journal version of the shoplifting-detection study (International Journal of Intelligent Systems, doi 10.1155/int/1947582) returned HTTP 403 and could not be read; all figures used (accuracy 83.59%, precision 82.46%, recall 84.62%, F1 83.53%, unseen-set 87.25%) are taken from the arXiv preprint 2408.00792v1, and the 87.25% is a violence-detection result on a movie dataset, not a shoplifting result.

NJ Legislature bill pages are JavaScript-rendered and could not be read for the Senate companion bills (S3182 in 2024-25, and the 2026-27 Senate companion that search results identified as S1464). Only the Assembly committee statements for A1494 and A3929 were read directly.
Could not confirm the New Jersey Data Privacy Act's exact effective date from the enrolled bill text I opened; the 100,000-consumer threshold and biometric definition are confirmed.
No New Jersey appellate decision quantifying damages for workplace camera deployment was located; LAD and wiretap exposure here is statutory and analogical, not case-measured.
NLRB GC 23-02's rescission by GC 25-05 is reported in NLRB memo listings but the rescission memo itself was not opened.

N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5.20 and N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.7 were both opened in this revision, but neither source defines which small independent practices count as 'covered health care facilities', so the buyer reach of the violence-prevention obligation is unquantified.

No public data found on how many small NJ businesses actually operate cameras, audio-capable cameras, or facial recognition — the demand estimate is inferred from establishment counts, not measured penetration.
Verkada camera-level licence pricing is not published on the vendor pricing page; the third-party pricebook figure seen in search ($249/yr) was not verified and is excluded.
No NJ-specific enforcement statistics on DCR algorithmic-discrimination complaints or FTC actions against small businesses were found.
The reported October 2025 FTC proposal to rescind the 2023 biometric policy statement was not verified against any FTC page in this pass and is presented only as unverified.
Vendor outcome claims (theft reduction, alert accuracy) were not independently verifiable and are excluded from measured_outcomes.
Frigate's release notes were not read in full for this revision, so no claim about accelerator/NPU support added in later releases (0.17+) is made here.
